title: Nothing in Between, or Enzymes in Between

scenes.tts: Why would a sensory cell accept being slow? A hair cell and a rod hold the answer.
scenes.visual: Title card: Nothing in Between, or Enzymes in Between. A hair cell on the left and a rod on the right, each with a question mark. Question on screen: why accept being slow?
scenes.narration: Why would a sensory cell accept being slow? A hair cell and a rod hold the answer.

scenes.tts: Every sensory cell turns a stimulus into a current. So the first question is what sits between the stimulus and the pore.
scenes.visual: A membrane with ion channels; arrows labelled force, odorant, heat and light arrive. Text card: Question 1. What sits between the stimulus and the pore?
scenes.narration: Every sensory cell turns a stimulus into a current. So the first question is what sits between the stimulus and the pore.

scenes.tts: In a hair cell, no enzyme. Bending the bundle pulls on tip links, and the pull opens transduction channels directly.
scenes.visual: A hair bundle tilts; a tip link tightens between two stereocilia; the channel at its end opens and ions flow in. Label: no enzyme in between, a direct mechanical link.
scenes.narration: In a hair cell, no enzyme. Bending the bundle pulls on tip links, and the pull opens transduction channels directly.

scenes.tts: In turtle hair cells, these channels can activate with a time constant as short as about fifty microseconds.
scenes.caption: In turtle hair cells, these channels can activate with a time constant as short as about 50 microseconds.
scenes.visual: A small current trace that rises almost at once. Label: channel time constant as short as about 50 μs, turtle hair cells.
scenes.narration: In turtle hair cells, these channels can activate with a time constant as short as about 50 microseconds.

scenes.tts: In a rod, there is a ladder of enzymes. Light activates rhodopsin, then transducin, then P D E six.
scenes.caption: In a rod, there is a ladder of enzymes. Light activates rhodopsin, then transducin, then PDE6.
scenes.visual: A photon reaches a rod disc. A ladder lights up rung by rung: rhodopsin, transducin, PDE6. Label: enzymes in between.
scenes.narration: In a rod, there is a ladder of enzymes. Light activates rhodopsin, then transducin, then PDE6.

scenes.tts: P D E six breaks down cyclic G M P. Channels close, less positive charge enters, and the rod hyperpolarizes.
scenes.caption: PDE6 breaks down cyclic GMP. Channels close, less positive charge enters, and the rod hyperpolarizes.
scenes.visual: A shower of cGMP molecules disappearing; cyclic-nucleotide-gated channels close; a voltage trace steps downward. Label: hyperpolarizes.
scenes.narration: PDE6 breaks down cyclic GMP. Channels close, less positive charge enters, and the rod hyperpolarizes.

scenes.tts: A mouse rod's response to a single photon takes of order a tenth of a second or more to peak.
scenes.visual: A single-photon current trace in a rod builds slowly to a peak. Label: of order 100 ms or more to peak, mouse rods near body temperature.
scenes.narration: A mouse rod's response to a single photon takes of order a tenth of a second or more to peak.

scenes.tts: On one time axis, the two sit more than three orders of magnitude apart.
scenes.visual: One logarithmic time axis from 10 μs to 1 s. The hair-cell trace sits near the left end; the rod trace near the right. Label: more than three orders of magnitude apart.
scenes.narration: On one time axis, the two sit more than three orders of magnitude apart.

scenes.tts: But one is a channel time constant, and the other a whole cell's time to peak. Read the gap as scale.
scenes.visual: Two tags appear over the traces: channel time constant (left) and whole-cell time to peak (right). Text: a picture of scale, not a measured cost.
scenes.narration: But one is a channel time constant, and the other a whole cell's time to peak. Read the gap as scale.

scenes.tts: Predict. What does the rod get in return for being slow?
scenes.visual: The rod ladder again, dimmed, with a question mark beside it. Text: what does slowness buy?
scenes.narration: Predict. What does the rod get in return for being slow?

scenes.tts: Gain. Enzymes keep working while active. In mouse rods, one absorbed photon removes about two thousand cyclic G M P molecules.
scenes.caption: Gain. Enzymes keep working while active. In mouse rods, one absorbed photon removes about 2,000 cyclic GMP molecules.
scenes.visual: One photon at the top of the ladder; a counter below runs up as cGMP molecules vanish. Number on screen: about 2000 cGMP per photon, mouse rods (Arshavsky and Burns 2014).
scenes.narration: Gain. Enzymes keep working while active. In mouse rods, one absorbed photon removes about 2,000 cyclic GMP molecules.

scenes.tts: That is one reason a rod can signal a single photon. Low dark noise and a reproducible response are needed too.
scenes.visual: Text card: gain is one reason. Two more items appear beneath it: low dark noise, a reproducible elementary response.
scenes.narration: That is one reason a rod can signal a single photon. Low dark noise and a reproducible response are needed too.

scenes.tts: A direct channel has no enzyme cascade before the current. Force acts on the channel complex itself. The rod's price is time. Molecules must meet, and enzymes must turn over, before any channel changes.
scenes.visual: Split screen: bundle force acts on linked hair-cell channel complexes and changes their opening probability (label: no intervening messenger-producing enzyme cascade; one bundle deflection can affect many channels). Beside it, the rod ladder with small clocks beside each rung (label: preparation-dependent encounters and turnovers).
scenes.narration: A direct channel has no enzyme cascade before the current. Force acts on the channel complex itself. The rod's price is time. Molecules must meet, and enzymes must turn over, before any channel changes.

scenes.tts: That is the one idea of this lesson. What sits between stimulus and pore sets what a sensory cell can do.
scenes.visual: Idea card: What sits between the stimulus and the pore sets what a sensory cell can do. Left: no enzyme, no enzyme cascade before the current; can be fast. Right: enzymes, thousands of molecules per photon; usually slower. Small print: speeds depend on the channel and the cascade.
scenes.narration: That is the one idea of this lesson. What sits between stimulus and pore sets what a sensory cell can do.

scenes.tts: The second question is how the signal leaves the cell. An olfactory neuron carries it on its own axon.
scenes.visual: Text card: Question 2. How does the signal leave the cell? An olfactory neuron with its axon running to the bulb. Label: primary sensory neuron.
scenes.narration: The second question is how the signal leaves the cell. An olfactory neuron carries it on its own axon.

scenes.tts: A hair cell or a type two taste cell hands it to a separate afferent fibre instead.
scenes.caption: A hair cell or a type II taste cell hands it to a separate afferent fibre instead.
scenes.visual: A hair cell and a type II taste cell, each passing a signal to a separate afferent fibre. Label: secondary receptor cells.
scenes.narration: A hair cell or a type II taste cell hands it to a separate afferent fibre instead.

scenes.tts: Together, the two questions make a table of four boxes, and five examples fill it.
scenes.visual: A two-by-two table assembles box by box. Rows: stimulus gates the pore; enzymes in between. Columns: primary; secondary. Entries: TRPV1 nerve ending and insect olfactory neuron; hair cell; vertebrate olfactory neuron; type II taste cell.
scenes.narration: Together, the two questions make a table of four boxes, and five examples fill it.

scenes.tts: Rods and cones do not fit neatly. They synapse inside the retina and send no axon to the brain.
scenes.visual: A rod placed between the two columns of the table, with a small flag: column disputed.
scenes.narration: Rods and cones do not fit neatly. They synapse inside the retina and send no axon to the brain.

scenes.tts: So ask two questions of every sensory cell. What sits between stimulus and pore? And how does the signal leave?
scenes.visual: Takeaway card: 1. What sits between the stimulus and the pore? 2. How does the signal leave the cell?
scenes.narration: So ask two questions of every sensory cell. What sits between stimulus and pore? And how does the signal leave?
